query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels in chemical‐processing and nuclear‐power applications is primarily due to the rapid formation of a chromium‐enriched passive film. This film forms by the selective oxidation of Cr at grain boundaries and is further enhanced by a high density of these boundaries, which accelerates Cr diffusion from the bulk to the surface, ultimately reducing local galvanic coupling and limiting corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional corrosion‐resistant steel (e.g., stainless or duplex steel) with a standard, relatively coarse-grained microstructure and baseline levels of chromium, nickel, and molybdenum as used in current chemical-processing and nuclear-power equipment.
generation.intervention: Apply a microstructural refinement treatment (for example, severe plastic deformation to produce an ultrafine-grained structure) to the baseline steel. This intervention is designed to increase the grain boundary density and thereby promote faster and more uniform chromium diffusion to the surface during exposure.
generation.conditions: Both the refined (ultrafine-grained) steel and the baseline coarse-grained steel will be exposed to controlled corrosive environments that mimic typical chemical-processing (e.g., acidic or chloride-containing aqueous solutions at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures) and nuclear-power conditions (e.g., high-temperature, high-pressure water or molten salt environments). All variables (temperature, pressure, solution composition) will be held constant between the two sample sets.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased density of grain boundaries in the refined steel acts as an enhanced diffusion network for chromium, leading to the accelerated formation of a uniform, chromium-rich passive oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of chromium occurs preferentially at grain boundaries. In the refined steel, the enhanced grain boundary network accelerates Cr diffusion to the surface, forming a continuous, protective Cr-enriched passive film that minimizes local galvanic cells and limits further corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse-grained steel, the refined steel is expected to exhibit a lower corrosion current density and a thicker, more uniform chromium-rich passive film under the same corrosive conditions, thereby demonstrating improved overall corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: The coarse-grained steel with standard microstructure and Cr distribution shows the usual corrosion rates and passive film characteristics when exposed to the controlled corrosive environment.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under typical exposure conditions for chemical-processing (acid/chloride solutions at moderate temperatures) and nuclear-power applications (elevated temperatures and pressures with corrosive species present), provided that the passive film integrity is not disrupted by excessive mechanical or thermal shocks.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of grain refinement versus inherent alloy composition in promoting passive film formation remains to be quantified. Variability in other alloying elements (such as Ni and Mo) and specific environmental conditions could also influence the corrosion response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: one set processed by severe plastic deformation to obtain an ultrafine-grained microstructure, and a control set with the standard coarse-grained structure. Expose both sets to a corrosive test environment that simulates typical chemical-processing and nuclear-power service conditions (for example, high-temperature pressurized water with controlled chloride content). Use in-situ surface analysis techniques (such as X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and scanning Kelvin probe microscopy) and electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization) to monitor passive film formation, composition, and corrosion rates over time.
measurements: Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization curves
Passive film thickness and chromium content via XPS
Surface potential differences using scanning Kelvin probe
Grain size distribution before and after processing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained (refined) steel does not exhibit a significantly lower corrosion current density or fails to form a more enriched and uniform chromium-rich passive film compared to the coarse-grained control, then the hypothesis that enhanced chromium diffusion via increased grain boundary density is the governing cause of improved corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
